If you act on nothing else

Both audits ran independently — code review and a live click-through — and converged on some of the same problems. Ranked by real-world impact for a tool that's about to get more than one user.

1
Deactivate or rotate sdd_test_admin
A live, Active, full-Admin account sitting in /admin/users right now — a leftover from this session's own build/verify work. Whatever password it holds should be assumed known. Flagged independently by both the code audit and the live walkthrough.
SecurityConfirmed live
2
Gate Billing/Invoices to Admin
Every other sensitive admin surface (Users, Settings, Message Templates) is locked to Admin on both the route and the API. Billing isn't — any Coordinator JWT can read, create, edit, or delete invoices today.
High · H1
3
Wire the sidebar's "urgent" badge to real data
It's a hardcoded stub reading "3 urgent" on every single page, directly contradicting the correct, live count shown one scroll away on Action Board and Admin Dashboard. Highest-visibility bug in the app — and the cheapest fix, since the real number is already computed.
UX · #1
4
Add rate limiting and size caps to the public quote form
No throttling, and no upper bound on the number of legs/services/persons or the length of free-text fields a single unauthenticated request can submit. Cheap to script, and it's the one endpoint anyone on the internet can already reach.
Medium · M1 + M2
5
Stop showing raw internal IDs to users
Strings like LEG-0004-1-FLIGHTPLANNING-ET-1787670722795 render directly in Trip Detail's deadline list and the Admin Dashboard's breach list. Swap in a human label; keep the ID as a tooltip if support needs it.
UX · #3
6
Sniff uploaded file type from bytes, not the client's claim
Paired with M4's CORS fallback — neither is exploitable today given the internal-staff-only audience and bearer-token auth, but both are one future feature away from mattering (a public upload surface; a cookie-based session).
Medium · M3 + M4
01

Security audit

Static, read-only review of the server — no live traffic sent, no files touched except this report. Full detail in .superpowers/audit-2026-08-26-security.md.

The core posture is solid for an internal ops tool with one public-facing form: bcrypt password hashing, a JWT secret that fails closed rather than falling back to a default, correct guard ordering, zero raw SQL, gitignored secrets, and a server-side upload allowlist. Nothing here is a Critical, exploitable auth bypass. The real gaps are authorization granularity — one admin surface isn't gated like its siblings — and a handful of hardening items on the one endpoint that's open to the public internet.

High

H1Billing/Invoices has no Admin gate — server or client
invoices.controller.ts:1-34 — no @Roles decorator on any route App.tsx:44 — /admin/billing not wrapped in <RequireRole role="Admin">, unlike Settings/Users/Message-Templates

Any authenticated Coordinator can list, create, edit, and delete invoices — through the UI (the nav item renders for non-admins) and directly via POST/PATCH/DELETE /api/invoices.

Billing is usually the most sensitive data in an ops tool. This is inconsistent with every other admin-only surface in the app, which suggests an oversight rather than a deliberate call.

Fix — add @Roles('Admin') at the controller class level (mirrors UsersController), and wrap the client route the same way Settings/Users/Message-Templates already are.

Medium

M1Public quote endpoint has no rate limiting
quotes.controller.ts:10-14 — @Public() @Post() No throttler/rate-limit dependency anywhere in package.json

A scripted flood of POST /api/quotes creates unbounded "Web Enquiry" trips — no per-IP or per-window cap exists anywhere in the stack.

Low-severity for a low-traffic B2B tool today, but it would quietly defeat this session's own "New Enquiries" triage feature under any real load, spam or otherwise.

Fix — @nestjs/throttler scoped to the quotes route, e.g. 5 req/min/IP.

M2CreateQuoteDto has no upper bounds
create-quote.dto.ts:107 — legs has @ArrayMinSize(1), no @ArrayMaxSize :112-122 — services/persons arrays uncapped; notes/client/service-notes have no @MaxLength

One public request could submit a quote with thousands of legs or a multi-megabyte notes field — whitelist: true strips unknown fields but doesn't bound accepted ones.

Compounds M1: no rate limit plus no size cap turns one HTTP request into an outsized database write and rendering cost everywhere that trip is listed.

Fix — @ArrayMaxSize(20) on legs/services/persons, @MaxLength(2000) on free text.

M3Uploaded file type is trusted from the client, not verified
docs.service.ts:48 — allowlist checked against client-supplied file.mimetype docs.controller.ts:28 — that same value is replayed as Content-Type on download, with inline disposition

Nothing sniffs the file's actual bytes. An attacker can label arbitrary content as image/png and it passes the allowlist, gets stored, and is later served back with that same declared type, inline.

Real-world impact is capped today — viewers are internal/authenticated staff, not the public — but it's a classic MIME-confusion pattern worth closing before docs get a wider audience.

Fix — verify magic bytes server-side (e.g. the file-type package), or at minimum force attachment disposition for non-PDF/image types and add X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff globally.

M4CORS reflects any origin with credentials when unset
main.ts:13-16 — corsOrigin defaults to '*', which resolves to origin: true (reflect the request's Origin header), combined with credentials: true

Because the JWT lives in localStorage and is sent via an Authorization header — never a cookie — this doesn't leak the token today the way it would for a cookie session. It's still an unbounded-reflection pattern sitting one future feature (a refresh-token cookie) away from becoming a real cross-origin credential leak.

Fix — set CORS_ORIGIN explicitly everywhere it's deployed (.env.example already models this correctly); change the fallback so an unset value denies by default in production rather than reflecting.

M5Trips/Persons/Legs/Services/Stops/Comms rely on client-side-only role enforcement
trips.controller.ts, persons.controller.ts, legs.controller.ts, services.controller.ts, stops.controller.ts, comms.controller.ts, person-ratings.controller.ts — no @Roles decorator on any

Any Coordinator JWT can write to any of these — the frontend's canEdit checks are the only finer-grained rule, and those are bypassable by anyone issuing raw requests.

This reads as a deliberate design choice, not an oversight — Coordinators are meant to operate on any trip day-to-day, matching how this session built leg-scoped crew/pax and reference data. Flagged for visibility, not as a defect: the same account could already do the equivalent action through the UI.

No change needed if "any Coordinator, any trip" is the intended trust model. Only revisit if per-trip scoping becomes a real requirement.

Low & Info

L1Unsanitized filename in Content-Disposition

The original upload filename is embedded in a quoted header value with no escaping — a stray " could malform the header for edge-case clients. Fix: use the content-disposition package for RFC 6266-correct encoding.

L2Audit trail is readable by Viewer accounts

Every field-level change, including presumably-sensitive billing/doc actions, is visible to the read-only Viewer role. Low severity for an internal tool; gate to Coordinator/Admin if Viewer is meant to be dashboards-only.

L3forbidNonWhitelisted: false silently trims unknown fields

whitelist: true already closes the actual mass-assignment risk; this only means client/server drift fails silently instead of with a 400. A defensible tradeoff, not a vulnerability.

I112h JWTs with no revocation

Stateless tokens, no denylist or refresh flow — reasonable at this scale, worth revisiting only if the threat model changes (shared/kiosk devices).

I2The one dangerouslySetInnerHTML call is safe

shadcn's chart-theming boilerplate, built from developer-supplied config — not end-user input. Confirmed not exploitable.

Already handled well — 9 things worth knowing weren't missed
  • Password storage — bcrypt cost 10, 8-char minimum, and a generic "Invalid credentials" error on both bad username and bad password — no enumeration.
  • JWT secret fails closed — read only from process.env.JWT_SECRET with no hardcoded fallback; a missing .env breaks signing rather than silently using a known default.
  • Guard ordering is correct — JwtAuthGuard runs before RolesGuard, so an unauthenticated request never reaches role logic.
  • @Public() audit came back clean — only login, the public quote form, and a stateless geo helper are unauthenticated. Nothing sensitive is accidentally exposed.
  • Zero SQL injection surface — no $queryRaw/$executeRaw anywhere; every query goes through Prisma's parameterized builder.
  • Secrets hygiene — .env gitignored, .env.example ships placeholders only, no hardcoded keys found anywhere in src/.
  • XSS — React's default escaping is relied on throughout; the one exception is confirmed non-user-controlled (I2).
  • Path traversal is eliminated by construction — uploaded files are stored under a server-generated ID, never the client's original filename.
  • The two admin areas that matter most for takeover — Users and Reference Data writes — are correctly Admin-gated, both server- and client-side. (Billing should have gotten the same treatment — see H1.)
02

Full preview & product critique

Eighteen screens, logged in as Admin on a fresh local build — everything from the public landing hero through every internal and admin page. Click any screenshot to enlarge. Full detail in .superpowers/audit-2026-08-26-ux-preview.md.

Landing / public flow

Holds up

  • The VIQ rebrand lands well — same accent, icon, and type weight as the internal sidebar. Doesn't read as bolted-on.
  • "Same form, pre-selected mode" works as designed: headline, prefilled Operation Type, and section visibility all correctly track the chosen path, and "← Back to Options" returns cleanly.
  • The Combobox that resisted browser-automation earlier this session turned out fine on a real click — a coordinate-precision issue in the testing tool, not a component defect.

Worth revisiting

  • Both hero cards carry identical visual weight even though Charter is very likely the majority path — no default/recommended nudge for a first-time visitor.

Core ops pages

Holds up

  • Composer is the best-organized page in the app — sparse, single column, clear optional-vs-required labeling.
  • This session's leg-scoped Crew & Pax rework is confirmed working end-to-end live, not just at the API — per-leg roster with a role-summary panel renders exactly as designed.
  • Audit Trail is genuinely useful: 379 field-level entries, searchable, with before/after values.

Worth revisiting

  • The sidebar's "3 urgent" badge is a hardcoded stub that never matches the real, correctly-computed count sitting one scroll away on Action Board (42) and Admin Dashboard (43). It's visible on every page — the single most jarring inconsistency in the app.
  • Raw internal IDs leak into user-facing lists — LEG-0004-1-FLIGHTPLANNING-ET-1787670722795 on the Admin Dashboard's breach list, similar strings on Trip Detail's deadline cards.
  • Manage Trips' default 72-hour filter shows "No trips match" against 9 real trips with nothing explaining why — reads as broken to a first-time admin, not filtered.
  • Leftover QA/test data is live throughout the seeded dataset — test trip names, a stray Task7 Mission Verify value sitting in a real Mission Type field, and audit entries attributed to sdd-cleanup/sdd-test/test. Not a code defect, but needs a cleanup pass before any real user sees this database.

Reference Data

Holds up

  • This session's search/Excel controls sit compactly beside each tab title without crowding the table — consistent across every tab checked.
  • Country Rules' new Add/Edit/Delete reads clearly; the Working-Days Yes/No pill is an easy scan down the column.

Worth revisiting

  • Airports and Countries are now manageable from two separate admin pages — Reference Data and Admin Assets — with nothing indicating which is canonical. Predates this session, but Reference Data just gained capability (search, Excel, Country Rules) that Assets' equivalent tabs don't have, widening the gap.

Admin

Holds up

  • The New Enquiries filter built this session works cleanly — the subheading, the filtered list, and the sidebar's live badge count all agree exactly.
  • Billing's empty state ("No invoices yet" + a prominent action) is a good non-dead-end pattern — worth reusing for Manage Trips' empty state above.

Worth revisiting

  • The Users page lists a live, Active, Admin-role sdd_test_admin account alongside a deactivated test_viewer_123 — a real access-control loose end, flagged independently by the code audit (see priority #1 above).
  • The urgent-count mismatch is unavoidable to notice here specifically — the Admin Dashboard puts the correct number (43) directly above the sidebar's wrong one (3).

README.md and ARCHITECTURE.md have already been updated separately to document everything shipped this session (leg-scoped crew/pax, Reference Data search/Excel, the landing page redesign, and admin enquiry triage) — this report is the review layer on top, not a substitute for those.
